name: Bwaidoka
confidence_why: Jenness & Ballantyne 1926 and Gibson 1992, two independent first-hand descriptions, both put Bwaidoka stress on the penultimate syllable by default and differ only in how far antepenultimate exceptions reach (a few words of more than three syllables for Jenness & Ballantyne, whole classes such as nouns with the intimate suffix, adjectives, numerals and colour terms for Gibson).

catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable on most words and generally on the antepenultimate syllable on certain classes of words: nouns which take the intimate suffix, adjectives, numbers and colors.

new_statements.quote: In the rapid flow of conversation some syllables are strongly accentuated whilst others are slurred over. Consequently it is often difficult to discover the value of the unaccented vowels, and especially of the final vowel with which each word ends.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: (1) Quote check. lines 2129-2132, between running heads 'LANGUAGE AND MEANS OF COMMUNICATION 57' (line 2100) and '58 LANGUAGE AND' (line 2144): "In the rapid flow of conversation some syllables are strongly accentuated whilst others are slurred over. Consequently it is often difficult to discover the value of the unaccented vowels, and especially of the final vowel with which each word ends." Verbatim (scanned double-spacing only). The chapter (ch. V, opens line 2058) explicitly takes the Mud Bay / 'Bwaidogan' dialect of Goodenough Island as representative, so identity for the 1920 quote is fine; the compilers characterisation (accent exists, no placement rule) is accurate for that source.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is given. The source only records that Bwaidogan has prominent (accented) syllables alongside reduced unaccented ones, and that the word-final vowel is often reduced. Where the accent falls (penult, initial, etc.) is not stated anywhere in the sources that could be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source notes only that unaccented vowels, especially the final vowel of each word, are hard to hear.
new_statements.domain_note: Remark is about connected speech ('the rapid flow of conversation'), not citation forms; ethnographic language chapter, not a phonology. Lithgow 1976:475 adds only cluster-level remarks (stress phonemic in Kilivila/Muyuw/Budibud/Misima; predictable within kinship nouns and verbs across the Papuan Tip Cluster) without naming Bwaidoka. Wikipedia (from Gibson 1992 OPD) confirms stressed vs unstressed syllables condition allophony but gives no position.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened material concerns the Bwaidoka (Bwaidoga) dialect of the southeast corner of Goodenough Island (Young 1979:vi; Jenness & Ballantyne worked at Bwaidoga/Mud Bay). Jenness & Ballantyne 1920 call the language 'Bwaidogan' and contrast it with Wagifa, Belebele, Kwaiboga and Kukuya varieties; Lithgow 1976 groups Bwaidoka with Diodio, Kalokalo, Yamalele, Fagululu in the 'Bwaidoka family'. Ross 1988 tags some 'Bwaidoga (Iduna)' data, i.e. the Vivigani/Iduna variety (idun1242), distinct from Bwaidoka proper. No dialect-level glottocode issue for the 1920 quote.

new_statements.relation_note: Same default as the catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate) and as Jenness & Ballantyne 1926 (work 2); adds class-conditioned antepenultimate exceptions (suffixed nouns, adjectives, numerals, colours), which is broader than Jenness's 'a few words of more than three syllables' but points the same way (the -na suffix does not attract stress). Header identifies the variety as Bwaidoka [BWD], Bolubolu, Milne Bay; villages Faiyava, Nikoko, Kobuna, Mataita.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable; antepenultimate on certain word classes (nouns taking the intimate/inalienable suffix, adjectives, numerals, colour terms), i.e. the final suffix syllable of those classes is skipped. The allophony notes on p. 3 also refer to vowel variants on stressed vs unstressed syllables, so stress is treated as phonetically real.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress 'generally' on nouns with the intimate suffix, adjectives, numbers and colours; no tone or length statement beyond the heading.
new_statements.identity_note: Jenness & Ballantyne 1926 describes the Mud Bay dialect of Goodenough Island (Bwaidoga proper) and notes neighbouring dialects (Wagifa, Kwaiboga, Belebele hills, Nufwasa, Fergusson Island) only for consonant alternations; Gibson 1992 is headed 'Bwaidoka Language [BWD], Bolubolu - Milne Bay Province', with data from the villages Faiyava, Nikoko, Kobuna, Mataita, population figure 'all dialects'. Both are bwai1242 / ISO bwd.

new_statements.quote: The accent, which is not marked in the texts, usually falls on the penultimate, especially in dissyllables and trisyllables and in words that are obviously compounded from two different stems. Thus ma'du and madu'ga "to run," mela'la "village," tagi'a "to weep," tagiafaili'na "to weep exceedingly," lakai'na "big," lakaivagai'na "very big." In a few words of more than three syllables the accent is on the ante-penultimate; thus bagaba'gana "corrupt, bad." Rarely it goes back one place farther, as in nua'dadana "to choose." In the word kadu' "again," the accent is on the last syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate at every length) and supplies the placement rule that the existing 1920 statement (Jenness & Ballantyne, The northern D'Entrecasteaux, p. 57) lacks; adds lexical exceptions. Describes the Mud Bay dialect of Goodenough Island ('the region from which nearly all the texts are derived'), i.e. Bwaidoga proper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (the mark is written after the stressed vowel) usually falls on the penultimate syllable, especially in two- and three-syllable words and in transparent compounds; a few longer words have antepenultimate accent, rarely one syllable further back, and kadu' 'again' has final accent (its fuller form kadu'we is regular). Elsewhere: the locative suffix -i, when it drops after e/i/u, lengthens and accents the preceding vowel (p. 296); in the compound anai'yegana 'his name' the accent is thrown back (pp. 302-303); kalivanai with antepenultimate accent means 'this man', with penultimate accent 'this/here' (p. 314 n. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult in a few words of more than three syllables (bagaba'gana 'corrupt, bad'); pre-antepenult rarely (nua'dadana 'to choose'); final in kadu' 'again' (fuller form kadu'we normal); accent shifted back in the compound anai'yegana; accent position distinguishes kalivanai 'this man' (antepenult) from 'this/here' (penult).
new_statements.identity_note: Jenness & Ballantyne 1926 describes the Mud Bay dialect of Goodenough Island (Bwaidoga proper) and notes neighbouring dialects (Wagifa, Kwaiboga, Belebele hills, Nufwasa, Fergusson Island) only for consonant alternations; Gibson 1992 is headed 'Bwaidoka Language [BWD], Bolubolu - Milne Bay Province', with data from the villages Faiyava, Nikoko, Kobuna, Mataita, population figure 'all dialects'. Both are bwai1242 / ISO bwd.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (not written in the texts) usually falls on the penultimate syllable, clearly so in di- and trisyllables and in transparent compounds (each example accented on the penult of the whole word: madu'ga, tagiafaili'na, lakaivagai'na). A few words of four or more syllables carry the accent on the antepenult (bagaba'gana), rarely on the pre-antepenult (nua'dadana); kadu' 'again' is final-accented, explained as a clipped form of penult-accented kadu'we.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated about secondary stress. (One war song in Part III, JPS 37(147), is printed with its stressed syllables marked because it was 'chanted.. to a trochaic rhythm so pronounced that I have considered it worth while to mark the stressed syllables' -- a metrical, not a lexical, observation.)
new_statements.exceptions: (a) antepenult in 'a few words of more than three syllables' (bagaba'gana 'corrupt, bad'); (b) rarely pre-antepenult (nua'dadana 'to choose'); (c) final in kadu' 'again' (< kadu'we); (d) p. 296: when the locative -i drops after a noun in e/i/u 'its influence is felt in the lengthening and accenting of the preceding vowel' (i.e. surface final accent on such locatives); (e) pp. 302-303: in the fused compound anai'yegana 'his name' 'the accent being thrown back in the compound'; (f) p. 314 n. 15 and vocabulary JPS 37(148): kalivanai with antepenult accent = 'the man here, this man', with penult accent (kaliva'nnai, n doubled) = 'this, here' -- an accent-placement minimal pair.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the speech of Mud Bay (Bwaidoga), Goodenough Island -- 'Mud Bay, the region from which nearly all the texts are derived' (JPS 35 p. 290); bracketed sounds from other Goodenough and Fergusson Island districts are noted but the accent statement is for Mud Bay Bwaidogan. Edition note: the copy read is the original Journal of the Polynesian Society serial (35(140) 1926 through 38(149) 1929), not the 1928 Memoir volume, which reprints it; cite JPS volume/page.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the default: Jenness & Ballantyne 1926 (JPS 35(140): 292) and Gibson 1992 (OPD p. 3) both put word stress on the penultimate syllable, matching the catalog rule. They differ in the scope of the antepenultimate exceptions: Jenness confines it to 'a few words of more than three syllables' (plus one final-stressed word, kadu') while Gibson says antepenultimate stress is 'generally' found on whole classes (nouns with the intimate suffix, adjectives, numerals, colours). These are compatible as a penult default with class-conditioned exceptions, but Gibson's version makes the exceptions much larger than the catalog's exception-free penult rule suggests. The 1928 Memoir could not be opened; it reprints the serial text.

sources.note: Section 84 'Stress', p. 475, is a survey remark on the Papuan Tip Cluster as a whole: 'Stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima, and probably also in Nimowa and Sud-Est. Stress is not indicated in any practical orthography. In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs.' Bwaidoka is not named in the stress section; no Bwaidoka-specific statement.
